transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-03-27 14:30 PST
- Duration: ~45 min
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Riya (Redwood CSM), Dr. Priya, Carlos, Sara, Tom (AegisPharm)

Summary:
Short sync to review week-over-week pilot metrics, dig into recent regression cluster on our scorecard, and agree on prompt pruning and next bench runs. Quick security check at the end re: KMS and data retention.

Topics:
- Scorecard deltas (precision/recall shift)
- Guardrail false positives and false negatives
- Prompt set pruning strategy and bisection plan
- Benchmark: hosted vs dedicated (latency/cost tradeoffs)
- Security ask status (SOC 2, KMS, VPC)

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Maya: alright, thanks everyone for joining, we—uh—wanted to kick off with the scorecard snapshot we pushed yesterday. Liam, you want to lead the findings?
[00:00:23] Liam: yeah sure, thanks Maya. We've been looking at the weekly eval runs, precision dipped about 6% on the safety guardrail, and we have a cluster of prompts that are producing higher false positives, looks like pharma terminology and some brand names are tripping the filters.
[00:00:42] Dr. Priya: that matches what we saw, the model tends to paraphrase protocol text oddly and the guardrail flags it as policy. It's not actual violation content, more like edge-case phrasing.
[00:01:02] Carlos: just to add, the dip coincided with the new prompt variant we rolled on Monday — shorter context, same temperature. Could be prompt engineering.
[00:01:18] Maya: ok, so two hypotheses: model behavior shift vs prompt set change. We recommended a bisection approach to isolate, we can run a targeted eval with the baseline prompt bundle and the new variant.
[00:01:35] Tom: can you remind us how long those bisection runs usually take? We have CI constraints.
[00:01:43] Liam: for the 1k-sample slice we did, about 30 minutes on Hosted; with Dedicated GPU and batching we can bring that to 10–12 minutes but costs differ. We'll add a short runbook.
[00:02:05] Sara: on the compliance side, the false positives are causing a lot of manual review overhead. If we can't tune thresholds quickly we need a temporary override to avoid slowing triage.
[00:02:18] Riya: noted, good to capture. We'll add a mitigation play — short term threshold relaxation plus manual spot checks.
[00:02:34] [00:03:10] Speaker 1 (Priya? mislabelled): ok moving on to the scorecard, Liam can you walk through the delta heatmap?
[00:03:22] Liam: sure. The heatmap shows the biggest regressions in the 'safety-sensitive' bucket and the rerank/intent detection area. Also, we saw token-level cost increase by about 9% for the same throughput — likely from longer completions after the prompt change.
[00:03:45] Carlos: yes longer completions, we noticed a small context leakage where the model repeats certain instructions.
[00:03:58] Maya: interesting, that links to batching/KV cache config too — if the KV cache isn't primed correctly we see warm-start penalties. Liam, can you check whether the cache TTL changed in the hosted config?
[00:04:12] Liam: will do. I suspect it's the session key hashing difference after the SDK patch. We'll validate.
[00:04:28] [00:05:00] Dr. Priya: about prompt pruning — our idea is to remove templated prompts that yield ambiguous completions and re-run evals. We can share 20 candidates.
[00:05:15] Maya: great, that's aligned with our approach. For pruning we suggest: 1) flag via scorecard (high false positives), 2) run bisection (old vs new prompts), 3) manual review on a 100-sample set, 4) finalize exclusion.
[00:05:36] Tom: what's the rollback plan if pruning hurts recall?
[00:05:41] Liam: we keep canary groups and a quick fallback rule to route to the previous model variant — Redwood's routing supports model variant fallback, so we can revert in minutes.
[00:05:55] Sara: on data concerns, will pruning or routing affect our audit logs? We need retention for 7 years for certain artifacts.
[00:06:07] Maya: all invocation logs will still be retained per the pilot config; we can ensure the audit entries for rollbacks are annotated. We'll double-check retention and exportability to your S3.
[00:06:21] [00:06:40] Carlos: can we also quantify the latency impact of keeping more guardrail checks? The product team needs numbers.
[00:06:48] Liam: yes — rough estimate: additional guardrail passes add ~8–12ms per request on hosted, but on Dedicated with kernel-level optimizations it's sub-3ms. We'll run a quick benchmark and include p50/p95.
[00:07:07] Maya: ok that's one of the next steps — benchmark hosted vs dedicated with current guardrail pipeline. We'll also show token-cost delta with our batching suggestions.
[00:07:20] [00:08:00] Priya: about scoring thresholds — can you explain the new adaptive threshold idea you mentioned in the doc?
[00:08:08] Liam: sure. Instead of fixed cutoffs, we compute dynamic thresholds per prompt family using historical precision/recall windows. It helps reduce false positives for families with naturally ambiguous language. The tradeoff is slightly more compute during scoring.
[00:08:27] Priya: that's promising — but we need to see the tradeoffs numerically.
[00:08:31] Maya: we'll include a small table in the CSV: baseline fixed threshold vs adaptive showing FP/FN and compute overhead.
[00:08:41] [00:09:15] Speaker 2 (mislabeled): question on eval scripts — are you using the same tokenization as our prod pipeline?
[00:09:24] Liam: yes, we tried to match your tokenizer; small mismatches were found in whitespace handling, which can nudge the score. I'll add explicit tokenizer parity steps in the runbook.
[00:09:39] Riya: also worth calling out, we observed one noisy prompt where brand acronyms were expanded differently which triggered safety heuristics.
[00:09:53] Maya: thanks, that will be in the shared noisy-prompts list.
[00:10:20] [00:10:45] Tom: can we get a quick recap on the false negative cases — are we missing safety flags or intent flags?
[00:10:53] Liam: mostly safety flags being overzealous (false positives). There were a few miss-classified intent examples in the 'adverse-event' detection where recall dipped slightly.
[00:11:10] Priya: for recall-sensitive cases we prefer recall over precision; those prompts should be whitelisted or rerouted to a specialist pipeline.
[00:11:22] Maya: ok we'll mark those prompt IDs as high-recall and recommend dedicated routing.
[00:11:34] [00:12:00] Sara: security check — last week we asked about KMS integration for key wrapping during private deploy. Any updates?
[00:12:09] Liam: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM; we've confirmed the connector for your vendor but need one more artifact from your side (key policy file). We'll share exact reqs.
[00:12:25] Sara: okay please send the doc. Also, is VPC peering ready for the on-prem test?
[00:12:33] Maya: we have a VPC peering checklist — we'll share it after the call.
[00:12:40] [00:13:15] Carlos: on the cost side, can you model the difference if we keep a lower temperature to reduce token length vs switching to a quantized 4-bit variant?
[00:13:26] Liam: yes two levers: prompt/temperature to control output length and model binary (quantized) to reduce token cost. We'll simulate cost per 1k requests for three configs: Hosted baseline, Hosted with temp tweak, and Dedicated with quantized model.
[00:13:45] Maya: reminder to include cache/batching settings since they materially affect cost.
[00:13:51] [00:14:20] Priya: action on our side — we'll produce the 20 noisy prompts and a short note on why they seem ambiguous.
[00:14:28] Tom: and we'll prioritize the 5 prompts that show highest manual-review impact.
[00:14:35] Maya: perfect. Any other blockers?
[00:14:42] [00:15:00] Riya: just a quick one — we recommended a temporary mitigation: a 'soft-fail' tag where guardrail flags are logged but not auto-blocked for a subset of traffic. That reduces manual triage while you iterate.
[00:15:12] Priya: sounds good but can we confine the soft-fail to internal users only?
[00:15:18] Liam: yes, routing rules can segment by account ID. We'll include sample config.
[00:15:34] [00:16:00] Speaker 3 (mislabeled): compression on the runbook links?
[00:16:07] Maya: I'll post links in the pilot folder after the call: scorecard CSV, noisy-prompts list, runbook for bisection, and the quickbench script. Link: /pilot/aegispharm/eval (note: placeholder link).
[00:16:25] [00:16:45] Priya: security follow-up — can you confirm if Redwood stores any plaintext PII in logs?
[00:16:52] Liam: we never store full request bodies in plaintext in hosted logs by default; we can purge or encrypt logs per your policy and route logs to your S3 with KMS. We'll document exact fields.
[00:17:10] Sara: okay please add that to the security artifact.
[00:17:20] [00:18:00] Carlos: one last technical: for the Dedicated benchmark, do you have a specific GPU/instance we should target to match our on-prem inference hardware?
[00:18:09] Liam: we can mirror an 80GB A100-equivalent setup; we'll also test a smaller 40GB node to show scaling. We'll send recommended instance types and expected p50/p95 latency.
[00:18:27] Maya: timeline — we'll share artifacts by 2025-04-01, AegisPharm to return bisection results by 2025-04-03, bench sync the week of 2025-04-07.
[00:18:44] [00:19:10] Priya: thanks all. Appreciate the clear next steps.
[00:19:20] Maya: quick recap: Maya to upload scorecard + guardrail one-pager, Liam to prep runbook and bench plan, Priya/Carlos to share noisy prompts and run bisection. Sara to confirm security items. We'll reconvene after those items.
[00:19:40] [00:20:00] End of recording — remaining minutes were quick side-channel chat and calendar scheduling.

References/Artifacts mentioned:

Notes on transcription quality: some speaker labels are approximate, a few technical terms were mis-transcribed (KV cache, canary->canary, HSM spelled correctly in sec notes), human names likely accurate.
